WHAT HAS HAPPENED, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN

The morning round is expected to strike at about 09:00–09:15, with its confirmed rates normally reaching us by around 09:30. At 10:36 they have not appeared, and our checks now record today's morning fixing as missing rather than merely late — the notice in the panel above is yesterday's lunchtime round, notice 310/26, struck at 12:04 on 12 August. It is labelled as such throughout, and no figure in this edition is presented as today's fixing.

To be plain about what this does and does not mean. It does not mean rates have moved sharply, or that anything is wrong with the market: gilts are trading normally and our estimates are live. It means the confirmed rates a borrower actually transacts at have not been published for this morning's round, so there is currently no morning rate to draw against.

It is the second consecutive day the timetable has been irregular, after yesterday's lunchtime round struck early at 12:04 — ahead of its usual window, which we corrected in the 12:52 edition.

THE MARKET HAS BEEN QUIET THROUGH THE DELAY

The market itself has been quiet through the delay. Gilt yields remain below last night's close across the curve, with the shorter maturities still leading:

  • 2-year: 4.287% (-2.0bp)
  • 5-year: 4.497% (-0.7bp)
  • 10-year: 4.958% (-1.1bp)
  • 20-year: 5.624% (-0.5bp)
  • 30-year: 5.704% (-0.5bp)
  • 50-year: 5.275% (-0.5bp)

Nothing has fixed, so these remain estimates: on live pricing a round striking now would come in near 6.011% on the 10-year (+1.1bp against yesterday's lunchtime round), 5.517% on the 5-year (+0.7bp) and 5.240% on the 2-year (+0.0bp) — the 2-year now level with where it fixed yesterday. The figures have barely moved since 10:15. The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — is 4.101%, -1.4bp on the day, with Bank Rate at 3.75% and the next move markets expect still a rise in Nov 2026.

WHAT TO DO ABOUT A DRAWDOWN TODAY

Treasurer's read: if you were waiting on this morning's rate to decide, the decision has effectively been made for you — there is nothing to transact against, and the realistic options are the lunchtime round, which strikes at about 12:25, or tomorrow morning. On the numbers that is not a painful place to be: borrowing costs have eased all morning and a round striking now would be little more than a basis point above yesterday lunchtime, with the 2-year level.

Two things to keep in view for the lunchtime round. NIESR publishes its monthly growth tracker at 12:00, shortly before the round strikes. And US producer prices at 13:30 land after it — so they bear on tomorrow morning's round, not today's.

We will publish the morning rates as soon as they appear, however late, and say plainly if the round turns out not to have been held at all.

THE MORNING’S RISE HAS UNWOUND

The 08:15 edition reported gilts higher at every maturity after the growth figures. That has gone into reverse in the hour since, and then some — UK government bond yields are now below last night's close almost across the curve:

  • 2-year: 4.295% (-1.2bp)
  • 5-year: 4.504% (+0.0bp)
  • 10-year: 4.96% (-0.8bp)
  • 20-year: 5.627% (-0.3bp)
  • 30-year: 5.705% (-0.4bp)
  • 50-year: 5.275% (-0.5bp)

The estimate for the round striking now has come down with them — 1.3bp on the 10-year and 1.4bp on the 2-year since the open. The shorter maturities are leading the fall.

AND THE BANK RATE VIEW HAS SOFTENED, NOT FIRMED

The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — is 4.105%, -1.0bp on the day, having been only 0.4bp lower at the open. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the next move markets expect remains a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: this is the opposite of what a growth beat normally does, and the shape of the move is the clue — the front of the curve is leading it, which is where Bank Rate expectations live. The reading that fits is that markets have looked past the headline to the weak production, construction and trade detail underneath it, and concluded the economy is not running hot enough to change the Bank's path. That is interpretation, not an observed fact, and a single morning is thin evidence.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE ROUND STRIKING NOW

Against yesterday's lunchtime round (notice 310/26, 10-year maturity rate 6.00%), the round striking now would come in +1.4bp dearer on the 10-year, +1.4bp on the 5-year and +0.8bp on the 2-year. Only becomes a rate at about 09:15, and the confirmed figures publish by around 09:30.

Treasurer's read: the day-ahead warned that this morning's estimate was stale and that a growth beat argued for a dearer round. Half of that has held — the round does still look dearer than yesterday lunchtime — but the margin has halved since the open and is now inside a basis and a half. For most drawdowns that is noise rather than a reason to wait; if you were holding off this morning on the strength of the growth number, the case for doing so is weaker now than it was at eight o'clock.

THE OPEN — gilts opened higher right across the curve after the growth figures; nothing has fixed yet, and the round striking about 09:15 would now come in near 6.027% on the 10-year, 0.5bp above last night's close

This morning's edition said the estimates on the page predated the 07:00 growth figures and that the open would give the first real answer. It has, and the answer is a mild one. UK government bond yields are higher at every maturity against last night's close — the 10-year at 4.973% (+0.5bp) and the 5-year at 4.511% (+0.7bp) — and the estimate for the round striking about 09:15 has moved up 0.5bp on the 10-year and 0.7bp on the 5-year since the close. Nothing has fixed yet. Against yesterday's lunchtime round it would come in +2.7bp dearer on the 10-year. One thing cuts the other way: the 1-year SONIA swap is 4.111%, -0.4bp on the day, so the market has not moved its view of Bank Rate over the next year even as it has marked longer borrowing costs up. Treasurer's read: a growth beat that nudges rather than shoves. The morning round looks like being modestly dearer than yesterday's lunchtime one, not materially so, and the gap is worth about a basis point of hesitation rather than a change of plan.

THE GROWTH FIGURES: SLOWER ON THE QUARTER, BETTER ON THE MONTH

Two readings of the same release, and both are true. On the quarter, growth slowed — 0.4% in the preliminary estimate, exactly as forecast, down from 0.6% in the quarter before. That is the reading the morning's press has led with. On the month, though, the economy did better than anyone expected:

  • Monthly growth: 0.3% (forecast 0%, previously 0%, revised to 0.1%)
  • Quarterly, preliminary: 0.4% (forecast 0.4%, previously 0.6%)
  • Annual, preliminary: 1.2% (forecast 1.1%, previously 0.9%)
  • Business investment, quarterly: 1.7% (forecast -0.5%, previously 0.9%)

Business investment is the eye-catching one: a rise of 1.7% against a forecast fall of -0.5%.

The production side of the economy tells the opposite story, and it is worth seeing before anyone calls this a strong release:

  • Manufacturing output, monthly: -0.5% (forecast -0.2%, previously -0.2%, revised to 0.1%)
  • Industrial output, monthly: -0.2% (forecast 0.1%, previously -0.7%, revised to -0.5%)
  • Construction orders, annual: -18.1% (forecast 11.8%, previously -11.9%)
  • Goods trade balance: £-23.01B (forecast £-20.5B, previously £-21.08B, revised to £-18.66B)

Treasurer's read: the growth came from the services side of the economy, not from factories, building sites or exports. For borrowing costs the headline is what counts in the first hour — an economy growing faster than expected reduces the case for the Bank of England cutting, and rates that markets expect to stay higher for longer feed straight into the price of PWLB borrowing. The weak industrial detail argues the other way, but it usually takes longer to be priced.

WHY THESE ESTIMATES DO NOT YET TELL YOU WHERE THE ROUND LANDS

This is the part that separates today from yesterday. Yesterday's two rounds were both struck before the day's big release. Today the release came first — published at 07:00, with the morning round striking at about 09:00–09:15.

Everything in the panels above was measured at last night's close, at 17:59. That means the estimates you can see are, quite literally, yesterday's answer to a question that changed at seven o'clock this morning. Nothing has fixed today, and no live market reading exists until the 08:00 open.

For the record, where things stood at the close, against yesterday's lunchtime round (notice 310/26, 10-year maturity rate 6.00%):

  • 2-year maturity: 5.260% (+2.0bp)
  • 5-year maturity: 5.524% (+1.4bp)
  • 10-year maturity: 6.022% (+2.2bp)
  • 20-year maturity: 6.565% (+2.5bp)

UK government bonds (gilts — the bonds PWLB rates are built on) closed yesterday with the 10-year at 4.968% (+0.7bp) and the 2-year at 4.307% (+0.9bp) against Tuesday's close. The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — sat at 4.115%. Bank Rate itself is 3.75%, with the next move markets expect being a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: if you are drawing down today, the honest position is that the morning round is less predictable than usual and the estimate on the page is stale by one news cycle. The 08:15 and 09:15 editions will carry live readings. If the certainty matters more than the timing, the lunchtime round gives you a second look with the reaction fully visible.

THE REST OF TODAY — AND WHICH ROUND IT REACHES

Still to come today:

  • 12:00 — NIESR monthly growth tracker (forecast 0.4%, previously 0.4%). Low impact, but it lands between the two rounds.
  • 13:30 — US producer prices, monthly (forecast 0.2%, previously -0.3%). High impact.

The timing rule matters again here, in the other direction. The morning round strikes at about 09:00–09:15 and the lunchtime round at about 12:25–12:30. A 13:30 release therefore reaches neither of today's rounds — it bears on tomorrow morning's. Anyone borrowing today can disregard it; anyone borrowing tomorrow cannot.

THE WEEK AHEAD

Next week carries the two releases most likely to move UK borrowing costs this month:

  • Tue 18 Aug, 07:00 — unemployment rate (forecast 4.9%, previously 4.9%)
  • Wed 19 Aug, 07:00 — UK inflation (forecast 3.0%, previously 2.6%)
  • Fri 21 Aug, 07:00 — retail sales, monthly (forecast -0.6%, previously 1%)

Treasurer's read: the inflation figure is the one to diarise. Markets expect it to jump from 2.6% to 3.0% — and today's growth beat, if it holds up, makes that combination harder for the Bank of England to look through. Both releases land at 07:00, before that day's morning round, exactly as today's did.

TWO ROUNDS, BOTH CHEAPER — AND BOTH BEFORE THE US FIGURES

Two rounds struck today and both came in cheaper than yesterday. The morning round (notice 309/26) set the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%, 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round. The lunchtime round (notice 310/26) took it to 6.00% — and it struck at 12:04, earlier than the usual 12:25–12:30 window. Our 12:15 edition wrote about that round as still to come; it had in fact already been struck, and we said so in the 12:52 edition.

The practical consequence was the good kind: both of today's rounds were priced before the US inflation figures at 13:30. A treasurer who drew down at either round took the rate without carrying the risk of that release.

Treasurer's read: the cheapest borrowing of the day was available before lunch, and it has not been available since. That is the second day running the morning half of the day has been the better half.

US INFLATION: EXACTLY AS FORECAST

All four US inflation measures landed exactly on forecast — an unusually clean result:

  • Headline, year on year: 3.4% (forecast 3.4%, previously 3.5%)
  • Core, year on year: 2.5% (forecast 2.5%, previously 2.6%)
  • Headline, month on month: 0.1% (forecast 0.1%, previously -0.4%)
  • Core, month on month: 0.2% (forecast 0.2%, previously 0%)

Both annual measures eased. UK government bond yields took a little more off the day in the ninety minutes that followed, and our estimate for the next PWLB round fell with them. That was the low-water mark.

THEN THE AFTERNOON TURNED

From about a quarter past two the move went into reverse, and by the close it had more than undone the morning. Yields on UK government bonds (gilts — the bonds PWLB rates are built on) finished higher on the day almost across the board, measured against last night's close:

  • 2-year: 4.306% (+0.8bp)
  • 5-year: 4.503% (-0.1bp)
  • 10-year: 4.969% (+0.7bp)
  • 20-year: 5.629% (+1.5bp)
  • 30-year: 5.708% (+1.1bp)
  • 50-year: 5.28% (+1.5bp)

The likeliest candidate remains the one this afternoon's edition named: a Gulf oil spill reported as the worst in years, with the Strait of Hormuz stand-off running alongside it. Yahoo Finance UK reported at 16:45 that UK shares fell on mixed US–Iran headlines. Higher oil feeds through to inflation expectations, and inflation expectations feed through to the price of long-dated government borrowing — which is where the biggest moves were.

The 1-year SONIA swap — in effect the market's live bet on where Bank Rate goes over the next year — ended at 4.11%, +1.5bp on the day. Bank Rate itself is 3.75%, and the next move markets expect is a rise in Nov 2026.

Treasurer's read: a day that opened as a cheap window closed as a slightly dearer one. Nothing in it changes the medium-term picture; it is a reminder that the discount on offer in the morning is not a floor to wait below.

TOMORROW: GDP LANDS BEFORE THE ROUND STRIKES

UK GDP is published at 07:00 tomorrow — the monthly figure, the preliminary quarterly figure and the preliminary annual figure, all together. Forecasts:

  • Monthly: forecast 0% (previously 0.1%)
  • Quarterly, preliminary: forecast 0.4% (previously 0.6%)
  • Annual, preliminary: forecast 1.1% (previously 0.9%)

The timing is the point. Today's two rounds were both struck before the day's big release. Tomorrow the release comes first: 07:00 publication, and the morning round strikes at about 09:00–09:15. Whatever the figure does to the market in those two hours will be in the rate the morning round sets.

The same Gulf disruption that drove this afternoon reaches tomorrow's figure from the other direction. Yahoo Finance UK carried a warning at 16:32 that the UK economy may grow by only 0.3% next year if Middle East disruption goes on — a forecast, not a figure, but it frames what a weak GDP number would be taken to mean.

Treasurer's read: if you have a drawdown pencilled in for tomorrow morning, this is the one morning this week where the 09:15 rate is not knowable from tonight's close. Weaker growth would ordinarily pull rate expectations down and the round with them; stronger growth the other way. If certainty matters more to you than a basis point or two, the lunchtime round gives you a second look with the figure already digested.

Nothing has fixed yet for tomorrow. On tonight's close the estimates stand at 5.259% for 2-year maturity, 5.523% for 5-year, 6.023% for 10-year and 6.564% for 20-year — each of them a guide to where a round would land if markets held from here, not a rate.

⚠ This reverses what this afternoon's editions said. At 13:55 and again at 14:15 the read was that the in-line inflation print had bought roughly half a basis point at ten years and a point and a half at two, and that the move was still running. It has since gone into reverse and then some. Anyone holding off a draw on the strength of that improvement no longer has it.
i The likeliest cause is not American. Agencies warned at 14:15 that a Gulf oil spill is becoming the worst in years — that landed almost exactly at the turn, and the whole week's direction in gilts has tracked oil rather than data. Equities are pulling the other way, with the S&P 500 opening in record territory after the inflation figures, which takes money out of bonds too.

The post-inflation rally has unwound, and the estimate has crossed over. An hour ago tomorrow morning's round looked like coming in near 5.991% on the 10-year, below today's lunchtime fix. It would now come in near 6.007% — above notice 310/26, which struck at 6.00%. That is a swing of about 1.6bp on the 10-year inside an hour, and the whole of it has gone the wrong way for a borrower.

The long end has given back almost everything. The 20-year gilt was 1.5bp lower on the day at 14:20 and is 0.3bp lower now; the 30-year has gone from −1.7bp to −0.2bp. The front end has held up better: the 2-year is still 1.5bp lower, from 2.8bp.

Where the curve ended the afternoon

Against last night's close: 2-year 4.282% (−1.5bp), 5-year 4.491% (−1.4bp), 10-year 4.953% (−0.9bp), 20-year 5.611% (−0.3bp), 30-year 5.695% (−0.2bp), 50-year 5.263% (−0.2bp).

On those levels the round striking tomorrow morning would come in near 6.007% at ten years, 5.511% at five, 5.236% at two and 6.546% at twenty — a touch above today's lunchtime rates at the long end, a touch below at the short.

Today, as struck

Two rounds, both behind us. Notice 309/26 at 09:07 put the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%; notice 310/26 at 12:04 took it to 6.00%, with 2-year 5.24%, 5-year 5.51%, 20-year 6.54%, 25-year 6.62% and 50-year 6.42%. Both priced before the US inflation figures, and on the afternoon's evidence that cost nothing at all.

Tomorrow is a UK morning

UK GDP prints at 07:00 — monthly, quarterly preliminary and annual preliminary, three high-impact figures together. That is before the morning round strikes, so unlike today the fixing will carry the number rather than precede it.

Worth remembering how thin the recent run has been: the economy grew 0.1% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and showed no growth in January. A soft print pulls the front end down; a firm one, against an oil story that is already pushing the other way, does not.

All four US inflation figures printed exactly in line. Headline 3.4% year-on-year against 3.4% expected, down from 3.5%. Core 2.5% against 2.5%, down from 2.6%. The monthly headline 0.1% against 0.1%, and core monthly 0.2% against 0.2%. Not one of them surprised.

Gilts have taken a little more off the day on the relief, and the move is concentrated where the risk was: the 2-year is now 4.272%, 2.5bp below last night's close against 1.1bp before the release, and one-year SONIA has gone from flat on the day to 1bp lower. The 10-year is 4.940%, 2.2bp down.

What actually printed

Headline inflation 3.4% year-on-year, from 3.5%. Core 2.5%, from 2.6%. Monthly headline 0.1%, after last month's −0.4%. Monthly core 0.2%, after 0%. Early reporting attributes the easing largely to food costs cooling.

Both annual measures fell and both monthly measures landed on the forecast. It is about as uneventful as a four-print release gets.

Where the curve sits now

Against last night's close: 2-year 4.272% (−2.5bp), 5-year 4.485% (−2.0bp), 10-year 4.940% (−2.2bp), 20-year 5.600% (−1.4bp), 30-year 5.678% (−1.9bp), 50-year 5.251% (−1.4bp).

The shape matters more than the size. Before the print the belly was leading and the front end was flat on the day; afterwards the 2-year has moved twice as far as the 20-year. That is a market unwinding a hedge against an upside surprise, not one changing its view on where rates settle.

Tomorrow morning

On the current curve the round striking tomorrow morning would come in near 5.994% on the 10-year maturity rate, 5.505% at 5 years, 5.226% at 2 years and 6.535% at 20 years — a shade under where today's lunchtime round struck.

The unresolved risk is the one that has run all week and is not American. Iran maintains there are no ceasefire discussions, the Panama Canal is charging a record $1m a crossing with Hormuz closed, and UK petrol is at its highest since the conflict began — against which OPEC has now cut its demand growth forecast for a fourth month. Gilts have priced none of it either way.

Our 12:15 edition said nothing had fixed yet and described the round as striking in the next few minutes; in fact it had already struck eleven minutes earlier and had not yet been published. Anyone who read that as time still available to act did not have it. The rates above are as struck.
i This round priced before the US inflation figures, as expected — with more margin than anyone planned. It struck at 12:04, an hour and a half ahead of the 13:30 release rather than the hour we set out this morning. Whatever prints at 13:30 now shapes tomorrow morning's round.

Notice 310/26 fixes the 10-year maturity rate at 6.00%, 2bp below this morning's round and 7bp below yesterday's lunchtime fixing. Across the maturity curve: 2-year 5.24%, 5-year 5.51%, 20-year 6.54%, 25-year 6.62%, 50-year 6.42% — 2 to 3bp lower than notice 309/26 at every point, with the belly and the long end giving up 3bp and the 10-year and 2-year 2bp.

On annuity terms the 10-year fixed at 5.57% and on EIP at 5.54%.

Where the day has moved

This morning's notice 309/26 struck the 10-year at 6.02%, itself 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round. Today's lunchtime fixing takes another 2bp off, leaving the 10-year 7bp below yesterday lunchtime and 9bp below yesterday morning. Two consecutive days of the oil scare unwinding have been worth close to a tenth of a point at ten years.

What the next round looks like

Against the new base the curve is now flat: on current gilt levels the next round would come in within a fraction of a basis point of today's lunchtime rates at every maturity. The market has stopped moving, which is what it does in the last half hour before a release it cannot call.

Gilts sit at 4.946% on the 10-year (−1.5bp on last night's close), 4.490% at 5 years and 4.284% at 2 years.

13:30

Four US inflation prints land together: headline expected at 3.4% year-on-year from 3.5%, core at 2.5% from 2.6%, headline monthly at 0.1% after last month's −0.4%, core monthly at 0.2% from 0%. The monthly headline is the swing figure — half a point of movement in a single month — and the geopolitical news through the morning has been oil-supportive rather than disinflationary.

Both of today's rounds are now behind us. The next fixing to carry the answer is tomorrow morning's.

i Part of the morning's improvement has already gone. An hour ago the same estimate stood about 3.2bp below the morning fix; it is now nearer 2.5bp. The rally into the print is being trimmed rather than extended, which is what usually happens as a release gets close and positions get squared.
⚠ The news flow is pulling the other way. Iran is reported as maintaining there are no discussions over a ceasefire extension because the pact no longer exists; the Panama Canal is charging ships a record $1m to cross with Hormuz closed; and the RAC says UK petrol has reached its highest since the war began. None of that has moved gilts yet. All of it is inflationary if it persists, and it is the risk to holding out for a better round later in the week.

Nothing has fixed yet. The round striking in the next few minutes would come in near 5.995% on the 10-year maturity rate — about 2.5bp below notice 309/26, which struck at 6.02% this morning. At 5 years it would come in near 5.513%, at 2 years near 5.235%, at 20 years near 6.542% and at 50 years near 6.433%.

This is the last round of the day that strikes before the US inflation figures at 13:30. Whatever prints then shapes tomorrow morning's round, not this one.

Against this morning

Notice 309/26 struck at 09:07 with the 10-year maturity rate at 6.02%, 2-year 5.26%, 5-year 5.54%, 20-year 6.57%, 25-year 6.65% and 50-year 6.45% — 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round.

On the current curve the round striking now would come in between roughly 1.7 and 2.8bp below that across the maturities, with the 20-year giving up most and the 50-year least.

The gilt market behind it

Against last night's close the 2-year gilt stands at 4.284% (−1.3bp), the 5-year 4.488% (−1.7bp), the 10-year 4.944% (−1.7bp), the 20-year 5.605% (−0.9bp), the 30-year 5.682% (−1.5bp) and the 50-year 5.253% (−1.2bp). One-year SONIA is 0.3bp lower on the day, having been 0.8bp lower an hour ago.

What lands at 13:30

Four US inflation prints together: headline expected at 3.4% year-on-year from 3.5%, core at 2.5% from 2.6%, the headline monthly figure at 0.1% after last month's −0.4%, and core monthly at 0.2% from 0%.

The monthly headline is the one to watch. A move from −0.4% to +0.1% is a swing of half a point in a single month, and the market's tolerance for an upside surprise looks thin given where the geopolitical news has gone this morning.

i Timing, not price, is today's decision. A 3bp improvement on a £30m draw is worth roughly £9,000 a year — real, but not on its own a reason to move. What makes the lunchtime round distinctive is that it is struck before the US inflation print rather than after it. Anything from tomorrow morning onwards carries the answer.
⚠ The front end has changed its mind. One-year SONIA was 0.5bp higher on the day at 10:15 and is now 0.8bp lower — a 1.3bp swing inside an hour. Short-dated expectations are doing more of the moving than the long end, which is why the 2-year implied is down 3.8bp against the 50-year's 2.2bp.

The curve has turned since the morning fix. Gilts have rallied about 2.5bp across the front and belly in the last hour, and on that basis the lunchtime round would come in near 5.988% on the 10-year — roughly 3bp below notice 309/26, which struck at 6.02% this morning. At 10:15 the same estimate stood about 1bp below the fix; the move has trebled since.

Nothing has been released to cause it. This is positioning ahead of the US inflation figures at 13:30, and it is showing up everywhere — gold near two-month highs, silver bid, European equities flat. The lunchtime round strikes around 12:25, an hour before that print, so it remains the last round of the day that prices without the answer in it.

Where the morning ended

Notice 309/26 struck at 09:07: 10-year maturity 6.02%, 2-year 5.26%, 5-year 5.54%, 20-year 6.57%, 25-year 6.65%, 50-year 6.45%. That was 5bp below yesterday's lunchtime round and 7bp below yesterday morning's, with the oil scare of the last two days still unwound.

What has moved since

Against last night's close the 2-year gilt is at 4.272% (−2.5bp), the 5-year 4.480% (−2.5bp), the 10-year 4.938% (−2.4bp), the 20-year 5.601% (−1.3bp) and the 30-year 5.679% (−1.8bp). An hour ago the 20-year was the one point on the curve trading higher on the day; it is no longer.

On that curve the next round would come in near 5.988% at 10 years, 5.506% at 5 years, 5.222% at 2 years and 6.538% at 20 years — between 2 and 4bp below where this morning struck, with the shorter maturities giving up the most.

The rest of the day

US inflation lands at 13:30: headline expected at 3.4% year-on-year from 3.5%, core at 2.5% from 2.6%, and the headline monthly figure expected to turn positive at 0.1% after last month's −0.4%. Four high-impact prints in one release.

The lunchtime round strikes before it. The next round to carry the answer is tomorrow morning's.

Overnight

Quiet, and quiet is the story. Last night’s wrap put this morning’s round 5.4bp below yesterday’s lunchtime fixing; it now sits at 5.3bp below, so the overnight session moved the estimate by about a tenth of a basis point. Gilts closed 2 to 3bp lower right across the curve — the 10-year benchmark at 4.962%, down 2.6bp — and the 1-year SONIA swap eased 1.9bp to 4.10%. The Middle East has not gone quiet: Iran and the United States clashed again over control of the Strait of Hormuz and equities were called lower on it. Treasurer’s read: the oil-risk premium that added 10bp to yesterday’s morning fixing is no longer transmitting into gilt yields — the market has stopped paying for the headline. That is worth watching rather than trusting; the same story reprices fast when a tanker is actually stopped.

Today's shape

Two rounds and one release, in that order. The morning fixing strikes about 09:15 and the lunchtime round about 12:25 — until the first of those, yesterday’s notice 308/26 rates stand. In between, an index-linked 2035 gilt auction at 10:00, low impact but the long end can twitch around one. On last night’s curve the 20-year would come in near 6.572% and the 50-year near 6.453%, each about 4bp below yesterday. Then US inflation at 13:30: 3.4% expected on the year against 3.5%, core 2.5% against 2.6%. It lands an hour after the lunchtime round has struck, so it shapes tomorrow morning’s fixing rather than anything priced today.

The week's real tests

Both arrive within eighteen hours. US inflation today is the one the oil story runs into, and the risk is two-sided: the Federal Reserve’s Susan Collins said overnight she would back a September rate rise if the data pointed that way, which is not the direction most had been leaning. Germany’s July inflation was confirmed accelerating, with core prices steadier. UK GDP tomorrow at 07:00 is forecast at +0.4% on the quarter against +0.6%, flat on the month against +0.1%, and +1.1% on the year against +0.9%. Treasurer’s read: a soft UK print pulls the front end down and would make tomorrow’s round cheaper again; a hot US print this afternoon does the opposite to the long end first. The Bank of England path is unchanged — a hold in September, the first rise priced for November, taking Bank Rate to 4.00%.

In local government

Andy Burnham said he wants to go “further” on business rates at the budget, and the City is trading talk of an early general election. Treasurer’s read: neither moves a gilt this week, but both sit on the revenue side of the same balance sheet as the borrowing decisions above — a business rates reform that shifts the local share changes what a council can afford to service, and an election changes the settlement timetable that most medium-term plans assume.

Tuesday 11 August 2026

17:15STORYend of day

A 10bp scare that unwound by lunchtime — the day ends with gilts below where it started, and tomorrow's round estimated 5.4bp under today's

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.07%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.016% (−5.4bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.535% (−5.5bp)1y SONIA swap4.099% (−1.8bp)

The day in one line. Borrowing costs rose sharply first thing on Middle East headlines, gave it all back by lunchtime, and drifted lower through the afternoon. Anyone who borrowed at the morning round paid about 10bp more than anyone who waited until the lunchtime one.

More

The two fixings. The morning round (notice 307/26) came in at 6.09% on the 10-year maturity rate, 10bp above Monday. The lunchtime round (308/26) landed at 6.07%. Both were struck while the Hormuz story was still moving, and both look expensive against where the market closed.

Where gilts finished. Yields are 2.2 to 2.7bp below Monday's close right across the curve — 10-year at 4.961%, 5-year at 4.506%, 30-year at 5.699%. That is the whole morning move reversed and a little more. The 1-year SONIA swap ended at 4.099%, 1.8bp lower.

What that means for tomorrow. On the closing levels, tomorrow morning's round would come in around 6.016% on the 10-year — 5.4bp below today's lunchtime fixing. The 5-year would be near 5.535%, also about 5.5bp lower. The 50-year would be near 6.454%. These are estimates from where the market closed, not a forecast of what tomorrow brings; anything overnight moves them.

If you are drawing down this week. Nothing in today's session changed the medium-term picture — market pricing still has the next Bank Rate move as a rise to 4.00% in November, not a cut. Today's fall is a retracement of a one-day scare, not a trend. The practical point is narrower: the morning and lunchtime rounds were 2bp apart today and 10bp apart from Monday's, so on days when a geopolitical story is live, which round you use is worth a moment's thought.

Thursday matters. UK GDP for the month lands at 07:00 on Thursday, with the market looking for −0.1% after +0.1%. A negative print would be the second weak month in a row and would sit awkwardly with pricing that still expects a hike. It is the first thing this week with the weight to move the long end on its own.

Council watch. The platform now carries a live calendar of every finance meeting on ModernGov with published papers. Fifteen fall in the next four weeks. Two of them — City of Lincoln and North Yorkshire, both on 18 August — have had their treasury papers read and written up.

15:25PULSEupdate

US housing data landed on forecast and changed nothing — gilts drift lower still, tomorrow's round now estimated 6.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.07%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.004% (−6.6bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.521% (−6.9bp)1y SONIA swap4.092% (−2.6bp)

US Existing Home Sales printed at 4.06m against a 4.05m forecast — as close to in line as these things come, and gilts did not react to it.

More

The afternoon drift has continued regardless. Gilts are now 3.6 to 4.3bp below yesterday's close across the curve, and on current levels tomorrow morning's round would come in near 6.004% on the 10-year maturity rate — 6.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing and 8.6bp below this morning's. The 1-year SONIA swap is 4.092%, 2.6bp under yesterday's close.

Nothing further is scheduled today. The overnight session and the Hormuz talks decide where tomorrow's round opens.

14:30STORYupdate

EARLY AFTERNOON — the day has fully turned: tomorrow morning's round now estimated near 6.014%, 7.6bp below this morning's fixing

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.07%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.014% (−5.6bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.526% (−6.4bp)1y SONIA swap4.095% (−2.3bp)

The day has fully turned. Gilts are below yesterday's close at every tenor — the 2-year at −3.5bp and the 10-year at −2.8bp, having been +7.2bp and +5.9bp when this morning's round struck. On current levels tomorrow morning's round would come in near 6.014% on the 10-year maturity rate: 5.6bp below today's lunchtime fixing and 7.6bp below this morning's.

More

Oil has given up its gains on optimism about the US–Iran talks over the Strait of Hormuz, though both sides set fresh conditions this afternoon. The premium that arrived overnight has more than gone.

Both of today's rounds are behind us. The morning struck at 09:08, the lunchtime round at 12:08. US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 and anything the Hormuz talks produce this evening reach the market after both — so they shape tomorrow's round, not today's.

The clearest read is the swap: the 1-year SONIA rate is 4.095%, now 2.3bp *below* yesterday's close against 3.4bp above it at the strike. A swing of nearly 6bp in what markets expect of the Bank of England, inside six hours, on no UK data at all. The Bank Rate path itself is unchanged — September hold, first 25bp step in November.

What today demonstrated: an 8bp round trip in the ten-year rate driven entirely by headlines about a waterway. Fixings are struck at a moment rather than averaged, so a council drawing at 09:08 paid about 8bp more than one drawing tomorrow on current levels. The Hormuz question is unresolved, so the same mechanism can run either way tomorrow.

The rate-path repricing has fully unwound

The clearest read is in the swap rather than the gilt. The 1-year SONIA rate — what markets expect Bank Rate to average over the next year — is at 4.095%, now 2.3bp below yesterday's close. At the morning strike it was 3.4bp above. That is a swing of nearly 6bp in what the market expects of the Bank of England, inside six hours, on no UK data whatsoever.

The Bank Rate path itself has not moved: no change is still priced for the September meeting, with the first 25bp step to 4.00% in November. What moved was the compensation demanded to hold gilts against that path — up sharply this morning on the energy-inflation scare, and back out again this afternoon.

What today has actually demonstrated

An 8bp round trip in the ten-year PWLB rate, driven entirely by headlines about a waterway, with no economic release involved at any point. That is worth filing away for the autumn.

Two practical readings. First, headline-driven moves and data-driven moves behave differently: a premium priced for an event that has not happened can evaporate as fast as it arrived, where a repricing built on an inflation print generally does not. Second, the fixings are struck at a moment rather than averaged, so a borrower's cost depends on which side of a headline their round happened to fall. Today the morning round caught the top; a council drawing at 09:08 paid about 8bp more than one drawing tomorrow on current levels.

The Hormuz question is unresolved — both sides added conditions this afternoon — so the same mechanism can run in either direction tomorrow.

What reversed

The oil-and-Hormuz premium that drove this morning's repricing has come out of the price. 11:19STORYupdate

MIDDAY LOOK — the morning's move is fading: the lunchtime round would come in near 6.085% on the 10-year, half a basis point below this morning's fixing

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.09%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.085% (−0.5bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.606% (−0.4bp)1y SONIA swap4.144% (+2.7bp)

The morning's move is fading, slowly. Gilts have given back about a fifth of it — the 10-year is +4.8bp on yesterday's close against +5.9bp when the round struck at 09:08. The front end led the move up and is leading the retreat: the 2-year was +7.2bp at 09:16 and is +5.0bp now.

More

The lunchtime round, striking about 12:25, would come in near 6.085% on the 10-year maturity rate against the 6.09% fixed this morning — about half a basis point better, and still some 10bp above yesterday lunchtime's. On £10m at ten years that is £500 a year: worth knowing, not worth reorganising a drawdown around.

The interesting part: the news got worse and the market eased anyway. At 10:36 another cargo ship was reported struck by Houthi forces in the Red Sea — the same shipping-and-energy channel that drove this morning's repricing. Yields fell regardless. That suggests what is actually being priced is the Strait of Hormuz specifically, not Middle East risk in general: Red Sea attacks are already in the price, a Hormuz closure is not. Watch the Hormuz headlines rather than the regional ones.

The 1-year SONIA swap supports that — 4.144%, up 2.7bp on yesterday's close but down from +3.4bp at the strike, so some of this morning's assumed inflation impulse is unwinding.

Nothing scheduled before the lunchtime strike. US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 lands well after it and bears on tomorrow's morning fixing.

For a borrower that is a small improvement, not a reversal. The lunchtime round would come in around 6.085% on the 10-year maturity rate, roughly half a basis point below this morning's fixing, and still some 10bp above yesterday lunchtime's.

At 10:36 another cargo ship was reported struck by Houthi forces in the Red Sea — the same shipping-and-energy risk channel that drove this morning's repricing. On the logic of the past two sessions that should have pushed yields further up. It did not.

AM FIXING REPORT — notice 307/26 fixes the 10-year maturity rate at 6.09%, up 10bp on yesterday's lunchtime round, on the oil-driven repricing

PWLB 10y — last fixed6.09% (+10bp)PWLB 10y — next fix est6.090% (0.0bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.610% (0.0bp)1y SONIA swap4.151% (+3.4bp)

The morning round has fixed. Notice 307/26, struck 09:08. The 10-year maturity rate is 6.09% against 5.99% at yesterday's lunchtime round — +10bp. Every maturity tenor is 9–10bp higher; the ten-year annuity and EIP rates are both +11bp, the largest moves on the notice.

More

On £10m over ten years that is about £10,000 a year more than the same draw yesterday, or £100,000 over the life of the loan.

This was the oil channel. Brent near $88 on a four-day climb and gold at a two-month high, after President Trump's new demands on Iran clouded the prospect of a deal reopening the Strait of Hormuz. No UK data was involved — the BRC retail sales monitor printed 1.0% against a 1.5% forecast, which pushes the other way.

The lunchtime round strikes about 12:25. Gilts have eased slightly since the morning strike — the 2-year is +6.1bp on yesterday's close against +7.2bp at 09:16 — so on current levels the afternoon round would fix at or fractionally below this morning's. Nothing is scheduled before it; US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 lands after the strike and bears on tomorrow's morning round.

Nothing is scheduled between now and then — US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 lands after it and bears on tomorrow's morning round.

The morning round has fixed. Notice 307/26, struck at 09:08. The 10-year maturity rate is 6.09% against 5.99% at yesterday's lunchtime round — +10bp. The whole curve moved with it: every maturity tenor is 9 to 10bp higher, and the ten-year annuity and EIP rates are both 11bp higher, the largest single moves on the notice.

This was the oil channel, as flagged an hour ago. Brent near $88 on a four-day climb and gold at a two-month high, after President Trump's new demands on Iran clouded the prospect of a deal reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The UK is a net energy importer, so the oil price feeds the inflation path and therefore the expected path of Bank Rate. No UK data was involved — the only overnight figure, the BRC retail sales monitor, printed 1.0% against a 1.5% forecast, which pushes the other way.

In cash: on £10m, a 10bp move is £10,000 a year. On a 10-year maturity loan that is £100,000 over the life of the loan, against the same draw yesterday lunchtime. A council with a £40m programme to fund this quarter is looking at roughly £40,000 a year of additional interest for having crossed one session.

Where the lunchtime round sits now

Gilts have eased slightly since the morning strike. At 09:30 the 2-year is +6.1bp on yesterday's close, against +7.2bp at 09:16 when the round was striking; the 10-year is +5.5bp against +5.9bp. That is a small give-back, not a reversal.

On levels as they stand, the lunchtime round would fix at or fractionally below this morning's. There is no scheduled UK or US release between now and the ~12:25 strike, so anything that moves it comes from the oil price and the Hormuz headlines rather than from data. Watch Brent and gold through the morning — they are the better real-time guide to the afternoon round than anything on the calendar, which is empty until tomorrow.

The treasurer's read

Labelled interpretation, not advice. Three practical points.

First, if you drew this morning, you paid for a geopolitical repricing that had nothing to do with UK fundamentals. That is worth saying plainly, because it is the kind of move that reverses as readily as it arrives — if the Hormuz question resolves favourably, a good part of the last two sessions could come back.

Second, if you have a drawdown scheduled for this afternoon, the honest position is that the lunchtime round currently looks like a coin-flip against the morning one, with no data to move it either way. There is no edge in the timing today; there is only headline risk in both directions.

Third, and most usefully for anyone with a programme rather than a single draw: this is the second consecutive session where energy has driven the front of the gilt curve, and the market is not yet pricing an earlier Bank Rate rise — the September meeting is still priced for a hold, with the first 25bp step to 4.00% in November. What has moved is the compensation demanded for holding gilts, not the expected path itself. If oil stays where it is long enough to reach the inflation data, that distinction stops holding, and the repricing gets larger rather than smaller. That is the risk worth planning around, not today's ten basis points.

09:16ALERTupdate

AM FIXING CALL — nothing has fixed yet, but the round striking now would come in near 6.099% on the 10-year, 10.9bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing, on oil-driven inflation fears

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.99%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.099% (+10.9bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.627% (+11.7bp)1y SONIA swap4.151% (+3.4bp)

Nothing has fixed yet. The morning round is striking as this goes out, and on gilts as they stand it would come in near 6.099% on the 10-year maturity rate — 10.9bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing of 5.99%. Every tenor is 10–12bp dearer, the 5-year moving most at +11.7bp. On £10m over 10 years that is roughly £10,900 a year in extra interest. The actual lands about 09:30.

More

This is an oil story, not a UK data story. Brent is near $88 after a four-day climb and gold has reached a two-month high, as President Trump's new demands on Iran cloud the prospect of a deal reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The UK imports its energy, so a higher oil price feeds straight into the inflation path and therefore into what markets expect of Bank Rate. The front of the gilt curve is leading — 2-year +7.2bp against 10-year +5.9bp — which is the signature of a rate-expectations repricing rather than a supply one.

How it built. Yesterday's close +4.8bp, 07:20 +5.0bp, the gilt open +7.8bp, now +10.9bp. Asia added two-tenths of a basis point; the London open put on 2.8bp and the hour since another 3.1bp. The move is still running as the round strikes.

Nothing in the UK numbers explains it — the only overnight figure, the BRC retail sales monitor, came in at 1.0% against a 1.5% forecast, which pushes the other way. Both of today's rounds fall before the only scheduled release: US Existing Home Sales at 15:00 lands after the lunchtime strike and bears on tomorrow's morning fixing.

How the move built

The repricing did not arrive overnight. It came in three steps, and all of today's part of it has happened in London hours:

When10-year estimatevs last fixing
Yesterday, at the close6.038%+4.8bp
07:20, before the open6.040%+5.0bp
08:20, gilts open6.068%+7.8bp
09:16, now6.099%+10.9bp

Asia added almost nothing — two-tenths of a basis point between yesterday's close and 07:20. The London open put on 2.8bp and the hour since has added another 3.1bp. The move is still running as the round strikes.

What it costs, by tenor

Against yesterday's lunchtime fixing, on the maturity basis, per £10m drawn:

TenorLast fixedEstimate nowMovePer £10m/yr
5-year5.51%5.627%+11.7bp£11,700
10-year5.99%6.099%+10.9bp£10,900
20-year6.54%6.646%+10.6bp£10,600
50-year6.41%6.513%+10.3bp£10,300

Annuity and EIP move with it — the 10-year annuity rate would come in near 5.677% against 5.56% last fixed, and the 10-year EIP near 5.647% against 5.53%. These are estimates, and nothing is fixed until the notice is published.

Underneath: gilts and Bank Rate expectations

Gilt yields at 09:16, against yesterday's close — the short end leading, which is what a change in the expected Bank Rate path looks like:

  • 2-year 4.392%, +7.2bp
  • 5-year 4.593%, +6.1bp
  • 10-year 5.047%, +5.9bp
  • 20-year 5.694%, +5.9bp
  • 30-year 5.781%, +5.6bp

The 1-year SONIA swap — what markets expect the Bank of England's rate to average over the next year — is at 4.151%, 3.4bp above yesterday's close, and the 6-month forward is 2.0bp higher. Markets still price no change from the current 3.75% at the September meeting, with the first 25bp step to 4.00% in November and a second to 4.25% in February 2027. That path has not moved today — what has moved is the compensation being demanded to hold gilts at it.

The treasurer's read

Labelled interpretation, not advice. Two things a borrower can act on. First, if you were planning to draw this morning, the decision has effectively been made for you — the round is striking as you read this, and the level is about 11bp worse than the last one. Second, and more usefully: the lunchtime round strikes about 12:25, and there is no scheduled UK or US release between now and then. Anything further before that round comes from the oil price and the Hormuz headlines, not from data. If the Iran story quietens during the morning, some of this morning's 3.1bp could come back before 12:25; if it does not, the lunchtime round is likely to strike around this level or worse.

For anyone with a drawdown that can wait, the thing to weigh is that oil has now climbed four sessions running and the estimate has risen at every one of our passes since yesterday afternoon. That is a direction rather than a spike, and it will keep pushing the same way until the Hormuz question resolves one way or the other — which is a headline risk in both directions, not a one-way bet.

Elsewhere this morning

The Reserve Bank of Australia held its key rate, citing elevated inflation pressures — the same energy-driven story reaching a different central bank, and a reminder that this is not a UK-specific repricing. European equities opened flat to slightly higher. Gold's two-month high and the four-day gain in oil are the two prices carrying the Iran risk premium at the moment; both are worth watching through the morning as the better real-time guide to the lunchtime round than anything on the UK calendar, which is empty until tomorrow.

InterContinental Hotels reported slower revenue growth and attributed it to the Iran war — the first UK-listed earnings this week to name the conflict as a direct drag, and a small sign the conflict is reaching the real economy as well as the oil price.

DAY AHEAD — nothing fixed yet: on last night's close today's 09:15 round would come in about 5bp above yesterday's lunchtime fixing, 10-year estimated 6.040%

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.99%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.040% (+5.0bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.566% (+5.6bp)1y SONIA swap4.12% (+4.0bp)

Gilts closed 6.5bp above Friday and nothing overnight has pulled them back. Nothing has fixed yet — yesterday's rates stand until 09:15. On last night's curve the morning round would come in near 6.040% at 10 years, 5.566% at 5 (the largest expected move), 6.587% at 20 and 6.460% at 50. The estimate re-anchors when gilts open at 08:00.

More

Overnight, two forces pulling opposite ways. Against higher rates: UK retail sales were soft, the BRC monitor at +1.0% year on year against 1.5% expected and 1.7% previously. For higher rates, and currently winning: a drone strike set fire to Libya's largest oil refinery, a second supply story on top of the Hormuz deadlock, with oil and gold near their highs and gold above $4,400. Australia's central bank held at 4.35% and said it had discussed a rise, not a cut.

Today is quiet, and both fixings come before the only scheduled release. The morning round strikes about 09:15 and the lunchtime round about 12:25; US existing home sales at 15:00 lands after both, so it bears on tomorrow rather than today. On last night's close the morning round would come in about 7bp above yesterday's 09:15 fixing — roughly £7,000 a year on £10m over ten years.

The week's real tests are still ahead: US inflation tomorrow 13:30 (3.4% expected, from 3.5%) and UK second-quarter GDP Thursday 07:00 (+0.4% on the quarter, from +0.6%). Bank of England path unchanged — September hold, first rise priced for November.

Overnight

Two things pulling in opposite directions, and the oil side is winning. Against higher rates: UK retail sales came in soft — the BRC monitor at +1.0% year on year against 1.5% expected and 1.7% previously, the weakest consumer read in some months. For higher rates: a drone strike set fire to Libya's largest oil refinery, adding a second supply story on top of the Hormuz deadlock; oil and gold are both near their highs, with gold above $4,400. Australia's central bank held at 4.35% but said it had discussed a rise, not a cut — a reminder that the global direction of travel is still upward.

Today's shape

A quiet diary. The morning fixing strikes about 09:15 and the lunchtime round about 12:25 — until then yesterday's rates stand. The only scheduled release of note is US existing home sales at 15:00 (4.04m expected, from 4.09m), which lands after both fixings and so shapes tomorrow rather than today. On last night's curve the 20-year would fix near 6.587% and the 50-year near 6.460%, each about 5bp up.

The week's real tests

Both still ahead. US inflation tomorrow at 13:30 — 3.4% expected against 3.5% — is the one the oil story runs into; markets are already positioning for it, which is part of why gold is bid. UK second-quarter GDP on Thursday at 07:00 is forecast at +0.4% on the quarter against +0.6%, with the monthly figure expected at −0.1%. A weak print there would pull against everything oil has done this week. The Bank of England path is unchanged: a hold in September, the first rise priced for November.

Monday 10 August 2026

17:22STORYend of day

END OF DAY — this morning's 09:15 fixing was the day's cheapest window; the afternoon undid it and more. Tomorrow's round estimated at 6.038% on the 10-year

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.99%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.038% (+4.8bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.563% (+5.3bp)1y SONIA swap4.12% (+3.9bp)

Three moves. At 09:15, notice 305/26 took every maturity 1bp lower — the last of the discount from Friday's weak US jobs report, and the cheapest moment of the day at 5.97% on the 10-year. At 12:15, notice 306/26 came back 2bp (50-year 1bp), more than reversing it and leaving rates a basis point above Friday's close. Through the afternoon, with no third fixing, the selling continued: oil rose almost 2% as the Hormuz closure dragged on, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose.

More

Gilts closed 6.3bp above Friday on the 10-year and 6.6bp on the 5-year, the day's weakest point. On that curve tomorrow's 09:15 round prices at 6.038% for 10 years, 5.563% for 5 and 6.587% for 20 — some 4.7 to 5.3bp above today's lunchtime fixing, and back above 6%.

For a borrower, this morning's fixing and tomorrow's estimate are about 6.8bp apart: roughly £6,800 a year on £10m over ten years. Nothing is fixed until 09:15 and an overnight reversal in oil would take much of it back.

This week: US inflation Wednesday 13:30 (3.4% expected, from 3.5%) and UK second-quarter GDP Thursday 07:00 (+0.4% expected, from +0.6%; the monthly figure forecast at −0.1%). Either can move the fixings by more than today did. The Bank of England path is unchanged — a September hold, the first rise priced for November.

The day in three moves

09:15 — notice 305/26. Every maturity 1bp lower, the last of the discount from Friday's weak US jobs report. 12:15 — notice 306/26. All tenors 2bp higher (50-year 1bp), more than reversing the morning and leaving rates a basis point above Friday's close. Afternoon. No third fixing, but the selling continued: oil rose almost 2% as the Hormuz closure dragged on, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose. The 5-year was the day's weakest point.

Where that leaves tomorrow

On the closing curve, the 09:15 round prices at 6.038% for 10 years, 5.563% for 5 and 6.587% for 20 — each roughly 4.7 to 5.3bp above today's lunchtime fixing. The estimate barely moved after 15:20, so the move ran in the European afternoon rather than building through the US session. It re-anchors when gilts open at 08:00.

What to watch this week

Two set-pieces, both capable of moving the fixings by more than today did. US inflation, Wednesday 13:30 — 3.4% expected against 3.5% previously. UK second-quarter GDP, Thursday 07:00 — the preliminary quarterly reading is forecast at +0.4% against +0.6%, with the monthly figure expected at −0.1%. A soft GDP print would pull against the oil story rather than with it. What the market expects from the Bank of England is unchanged after all of this: a hold in September, the first rise priced for November.

The sell-off that doubled between 14:24 and 15:20 has gone sideways since. The 10-year gilt is 4.98%, within a fifth of a basis point of where it sat an hour ago, and the whole curve is unchanged: still 5 to 6bp above Friday's close.

More

That leaves tomorrow's 09:15 round priced at 6.033% for the 10-year and 5.558% for the 5-year — effectively where the 15:20 read left it. The move ran in the European afternoon and has not extended into the US session.

15:20STORYupdate

AFTERNOON SELL-OFF ACCELERATES — oil up 2% and US yields rising put tomorrow's 09:15 round at 6.034% on the 10-year, back above 6% and 4.4bp above today's lunchtime fixing

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.99%PWLB 10y — next fix est6.034% (+4.4bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.559% (+4.9bp)1y SONIA swap4.12% (+4.2bp)

The move has doubled in the last hour. At 14:24 tomorrow morning's round was priced 1.7bp above today's lunchtime fixing; it is now 4.4bp above, and back above 6% on the 10-year for the first time today.

More

One story, three transmissions: oil rose almost 2% as the Gulf hardened its position on Hormuz, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose, and the UK curve took both cues. Gilts are now 5 to 6bp above Friday's close across every maturity, with the 5-year weakest at +6.2bp — the belly leading, which is where a rate path gets repriced rather than a risk premium. One-year SONIA is 4.2bp higher on the day.

Measured against this morning's fixing at 5.97%, tomorrow is currently 6.4bp dearer — around £6,400 a year on £10m over ten years. Two caveats: this is an estimate seventeen hours before the strike, and an overnight reversal in oil would unwind much of it. Nothing has fixed — today's rates stand until 09:15.

Neither of the week's set-pieces has landed. US inflation Wednesday 13:30 and UK second-quarter GDP Thursday 07:00 can each move the fixings by more than this whole day has.

⚠ The move has doubled in the last hour. At 14:24 tomorrow's round was priced 1.7bp above today's; it is now 4.4bp above. Measured against this morning's fixing at 5.97%, tomorrow is currently 6.4bp dearer — roughly £6,400 a year on £10m over ten years.

The sell-off has accelerated through the afternoon. Oil is up almost 2% with the Hormuz stalemate unresolved, US shares opened lower and Treasury yields rose — and UK gilts have followed, now 5 to 6 basis points above Friday's close right across the curve. Tomorrow's 09:15 fixing is currently estimated at 6.034% for the 10-year, back above 6% and 4.4bp above today's lunchtime round.

What is driving it

One story, three transmissions. Oil rose almost 2% as the Gulf hardened its position on Hormuz, which lifts the inflation path; US Treasury yields rose with it; and the UK curve, which has tracked the oil story all day, took both cues. The 5-year gilt is the day's weakest point at +6.2bp, with the 10-year at +6.0bp and the 2-year +5.4bp — the belly of the curve leading, which is where a rate path gets repriced rather than a risk premium. One-year SONIA is 4.2bp higher on the day.

What it means for tomorrow

On these levels the morning round would print near 6.034% at 10 years, 5.559% at 5 and 6.578% at 20 — each about 4 to 5bp above today's lunchtime fixing. Two caveats worth holding onto. This is an estimate made seventeen hours before the strike, and an overnight reversal in oil would unwind much of it; the estimate re-anchors when the gilt market opens at 08:00. And nothing has actually fixed — today's rates stand until 09:15.

The week ahead

Neither of the week's set-pieces has landed yet. US inflation lands Wednesday at 13:30 — 3.4% expected, down from 3.5% — and UK second-quarter GDP on Thursday at 07:00, forecast at +0.4% against +0.6% previously. Either can move the fixings by more than everything that has happened today. What the market expects from the Bank of England is still a September hold with the first rise priced for November.

What moved it

Gilts sold off steadily through the morning as the Hormuz talks stayed stuck and oil held its gains. By lunchtime the 10-year gilt yield was 4.94%, up 1.5bp on Friday's close, and the 2-year was up 2.0bp — the front end took the larger hit, which is the market trimming its enthusiasm for near-term easing rather than repricing the long end. The PWLB fixing simply followed: it is set off the gilt curve at the moment it is struck, and the curve at 12:15 was higher than the curve at 09:15.

How our call did

The 12:19 estimate said this round would land 0.8 to 1.5bp above the morning fixing. It landed 2bp above — the direction was right and the size was about a basis point light. Across the five benchmark maturities the estimates were between 0.2 and 1.1bp below the printed rates, all in the same direction. Worth logging honestly: on a day when the market is moving one way all morning, our estimates lag the move slightly rather than overshooting it.

What happens next

That is both of today's fixings done — the next reset is tomorrow at 09:15, and it is currently priced flat to half a basis point above this afternoon's levels. There is no scheduled UK or US data left today, so anything that moves tomorrow morning's round will come from the oil story overnight. The week's real set-pieces are still ahead: US inflation on Wednesday at 13:30 (3.4% expected, down from 3.5%) and UK second-quarter GDP on Thursday at 07:00 (+0.4% expected, down from +0.6%). Either is capable of moving the fixings by more than today's 2bp. What the market expects from the Bank of England is unchanged: a hold in September, the first rise priced for November.

How it happened

Friday 13:30: the US reported losing 23,000 jobs against an expected 80,000 gain, and UK market rates fell with global ones. Over the weekend the other force arrived: Hormuz talks stalled, oil climbed, and this morning's gilt open gave back most — but not all — of the jobs-shock fall. What survived into the 09:15 strike was worth one basis point. For context, the week-on-week move is modest: the 10-year standard rate is 3bp above last Monday's level.

For borrowing decisions

A borrower who waited from Friday saved a basis point — and nothing in the current market argues for rushing before lunch: the ~12:25 round is priced level with this morning's. The bigger swings this week are scheduled, not drifting: US inflation Wednesday and UK second-quarter GDP Thursday 07:00 are each capable of moving the next fixings by more than today's move. What markets expect from the Bank of England is unchanged today: a September hold, with the first rise still priced for November.

07:50STORYmorning brief

Morning brief — Monday opens roughly level with Friday's PM fix; Hormuz stand-off runs on, China inflation cools; no UK data until Wednesday's GDP

PWLB 10y — last fixed5.98%PWLB 10y — next fix est5.975% (−0.5bp)PWLB 5y — next fix est5.497% (−0.3bp)1y SONIA swap4.077% (−1.8bp)

Markets pick up almost exactly where Friday's close left them: the engine's next-fix estimate sits within a basis point of Friday's PM fixing across the curve, matching Friday's End of Day call that Monday would open roughly level after two fixings and a US jobs shock. No UK data is due today — the next release is Wednesday's GDP figures. The PWLB 10-year fixed at 5.98% on Friday afternoon (PM, notice 304/26); today's AM fixing is due ~09:00–09:15 UK and will reset the estimate once gilts open at 08:00.

More

Weekend and overnight. The Iran-Hormuz story live in Friday's brief remains unresolved: this morning's wires report no Hormuz deal in sight, oil prices extending gains, and the US reportedly shifting toward economic pressure on Iran rather than further military action. Treasurer's read: a longer stand-off keeps a floor under oil prices — a modest headwind for the disinflation story markets have been pricing — but it has not moved UK gilts or the Bank Rate path so far.

Overnight, China's headline inflation cooled to 0.5% year-on-year (forecast 0.8%, prior 1%), a bigger slowdown than expected and read by wires as a sign the Iran-war oil shock is fading through China's economy. Treasurer's read: softer Chinese price pressure adds to the global disinflation case that has been supporting gilts recently, though the direct UK-rates read-through is limited.

The week ahead. No UK data today. Wednesday's preliminary GDP (07:00 UK) is the next release: growth is forecast to slow sharply on the quarter (+0.4% vs +0.6% previously), while the year-on-year rate is forecast to pick up to 1.6% from 0.9% on base effects. A weaker-than-forecast reading would likely pull gilt yields down and ease the estimated cost of new borrowing; a stronger one would do the reverse. Bank Rate path unchanged: hold in September, +25bp priced for November 2026.

Markets pick up almost exactly where Friday's close left them: the engine's next-fix estimate sits within a basis point of Friday's PM fixing across the curve, matching Friday's End of Day call that Monday would open roughly level after two fixings and a US jobs shock. There is no UK data due today — the next release is Wednesday's GDP figures. Weekend and overnight: oil stand-off runs on, China's inflation cools

The Iran-Hormuz story that was live in Friday's brief is still unresolved: this morning's wires report no Hormuz deal in sight, with oil prices extending their gains and the US reportedly shifting toward economic pressure on Iran rather than further military action. Treasurer's read: a longer stand-off keeps a floor under oil prices — a modest headwind for the disinflation story markets have been pricing — but it has not moved UK gilts or the Bank Rate path so far.

Treasurer's read: softer Chinese price pressure adds to the global disinflation case that has been supporting gilts recently, though the direct UK-rates read-through is limited — worth watching for confirmation in this week's releases.

The next release is Wednesday's preliminary GDP (07:00 UK): the market expects growth to have slowed sharply on the quarter — +0.4% forecast, down from +0.6% previously — while the year-on-year rate is forecast to pick up to 1.6% from 0.9% on base effects. ⚠ Read the panel as Friday's baseline, not this morning's market. Estimates are anchored to Friday's close; the gilt market reopens at 08:00 and will reprice them live before the ~09:15 fixing. With oil up on the failed Hormuz talks, the risk to these numbers this morning sits on the upside.

The weekend's big hope didn't land: there is no Strait of Hormuz deal — Iranian demands have hardened, Washington is talking economic pressure after fresh strikes, and oil is extending gains into Monday. Against that, Friday's US jobs shock is still in the price: our estimates for this morning's ~09:15 fixing sit 0.3–1.2bp below Friday's rates across the board — 10-year standard at 5.975% against Friday's 5.98% fixing. A quiet UK Monday (no releases) starts a loud week: US inflation Wednesday, UK second-quarter GDP Thursday.

This morning's fixing

The AM round strikes ~09:00–09:15 and the confirmed rates are published by ~09:30; we'll report them with a deep-dive as soon as they land. Friday's pattern was a round trip — fixed at 6.00% in the morning, 5.98% at lunch, then the jobs shock pulled market rates lower still — and the portion that stuck is what today's estimates carry. For borrowing decisions: nothing here argues for urgency; if the oil move firms rates at the open, today's fixing likely lands at or a shade above Friday's — the afternoon will tell us more than the morning.

The weekend, in brief

Hormuz: no deal. Talks that looked close on Friday have stalled on Iranian demands; the US president signalled a shift to economic pressure over further military strikes, and oil rose through Asian trading. For UK rates this is the inflationary tail-risk staying alive — it is the main argument against the market's post-jobs softness.

China's inflation cooled — July CPI rose 0.5% on the year against 0.8% expected, early evidence the oil shock's pass-through is easing there. Mildly reassuring for global rates, including ours.

Elsewhere: Russian missile strikes near Kyiv killed three on Saturday, keeping the escalation risk we flagged on Friday live; Typhoon Dolphin hit Japan and is heading for China's coast (watch supply-chain noise, limited direct gilt impact); and at home, North Sea oil politics sharpened ahead of conference season — a fiscal story eventually, not a rates story today.

The week ahead

Today: no UK releases — the fixing is the day's event. Wednesday: US July inflation, the release most likely to move UK rates from abroad; a hot print would test how much of Friday's relief survives. Thursday 07:00: UK second-quarter GDP, first estimate — an awkward, two-handed forecast: the year-on-year rate is expected to jump to 1.6% (from 0.9%), but June's month alone is forecast at −0.1%. A strong headline supports the November rate-rise pricing; a soft June month gives the doves their counter. We'll arm an event pass for both.

i New: the WEEKEND READ. A Saturday-morning edition — slower, longer, no live feed to chase. The week in review, then one or two carefully chosen research pieces from central banks, think tanks and investment desks, each with a plain explanation of why it earns your time. This pilot was produced Friday evening; from next week it files Saturdays around 10:00.

A week that ran up the stairs and came back down the escalator. PWLB borrowing costs climbed steadily into Friday morning — the 10-year standard rate touched 6.00% at the AM fixing, its highest of the run — before a shock US jobs report (23,000 jobs lost against 80,000 expected) pulled market rates back and left Monday's estimated fixing almost exactly where Friday's ended: 10-year at 5.975%. Net on the week, the 10-year standard rate is about 4bp higher. This is the first WEEKEND READ — the week's story in full, the numbers that matter, and two pieces of research worth your time with a cup of coffee.

The week — up the stairs, down the escalator

The watch joined mid-week, so the story starts Thursday: gilt yields rose 4–6bp on the day and PWLB rates followed at Friday morning's fixing — up 4–6bp across the board, the 10-year standard rate printing 6.00% and the 20-year 6.56%. The push had global fingerprints: energy-supply nerves around the Strait of Hormuz, a China export beat, US chip-tariff noise, and a US Federal Reserve whose last meeting produced three dissents in favour of an immediate rate rise.

Friday told the other half of the story. The lunchtime fixing eased 1–2bp (10-year to 5.98%), and at 13:30 UK the US reported losing 23,000 jobs against an expected 80,000 gain — the kind of miss that changes minds. Market rates fell sharply, UK expectations followed, and although the move faded through the afternoon (markets gave back roughly two-thirds of it), the week closed with gilt yields 0.9–1.9bp lower on the day and the rise the market prices from the Bank of England pushed a little further out.

Where that leaves the Bank of England picture: Bank Rate stays 3.75% now; September is priced as a hold; the first rise is priced for November; and the second hovers around the turn of Q1 2027 — its timing visibly finely balanced, flickering between March and April as Friday's data landed. For borrowing decisions: Monday's estimated fixings sit 0.3–1.1bp below Friday's — essentially level — so nothing in the data argues for urgency either way; the weekend's Hormuz and Ukraine headlines are the wildcard that could reset Monday's open.

Worth your time — two reads
Bank of England · Bank Insights · 17 July 2026 · ~8 min
Bank Rate expectations in the UK curve following the war in Iran

Two Bank staff economists, Andras Lengyel and Danny Walker, examine the same market curve our “what markets expect the Bank of England to do” panel is built from — and argue it currently overstates the chance of rate rises. Stripping out risk premium with a term-structure model, they find the model-implied Bank Rate path is “broadly flat over the next year”, in line with what surveyed market participants actually say they expect. The upward slope, on this reading, is mostly compensation for uncertainty — at levels unusual outside 2022–23 — rather than a genuine forecast of hikes.

Why it earns your time: our brief has reported a first rise priced for November all week. This is the strongest public argument that pricing like that can flatter the true odds — which cuts both ways for a borrower: less reason to rush a drawdown to “beat” November, but also a reminder that curve-implied paths can deflate quickly, exactly as Friday afternoon showed.

NIESR · David Aikman · 9 January 2026 · ~11 min
Could a gilt market shock derail the economy in 2026?

Written in January, when the consensus saw gilt yields drifting down toward 4.4% — a central case the year has comprehensively overtaken. Read it instead for the risk half, which has aged remarkably well: a step-by-step map of how a yield repricing becomes a market spiral — leveraged trades unwinding, repo funding tightening, redemptions from the non-bank funds that now dominate gilt-market liquidity — and why the Bank of England faces a genuine dilemma about intervening without becoming a standing backstop.

Why it earns your time: the January “risk scenario” is a fair description of the world since February's war. For a treasurer, its value is the transmission map — what a bad fortnight in gilts does to PWLB rates, how fast, and why “wait for it to blow over” has not always been a safe strategy in this market structure. Note the date throughout: it is a framework piece, not a current forecast.

Selection standard: freely accessible at time of writing, read in full before inclusion, publication date always shown. Sources this week were checked against fresher weekly commentary (BlackRock Investment Institute and peers); these two won on substance.

The week ahead

Monday ~09:15 — the AM fixing, first test of the jobs-shock repricing; our estimates say 0.3–1.1bp below Friday. Wednesday — US July inflation, the global release most likely to move UK rates mid-week. Thursday 07:00 UK — second-quarter GDP, first estimate: forecasts have year-on-year growth accelerating to 1.6% from 0.9%, which — if delivered — supports the case for that November rise; a miss would feed the doves. Weekend wildcards: the reported Hormuz de-escalation deal and Ukraine, either of which could reset Monday's open before any data lands.

PWLB 10-year fixed at 6.00% in the morning and 5.98% at lunchtime; the weak US jobs report then knocked market rates sharply lower — before most of that move faded through the afternoon. Our estimates for Monday's ~09:15 fixing sit 0.3–1.1bp under Friday's lunchtime rates: close to level.

The day, start to finish
The morning edition flagged an overnight rise carrying into the first fixing, and it landed: the AM round (notice 303/26, 09:06) rose 4–6bp, with PWLB 10-year standard touching 6.00%. The lunchtime round (304/26, 12:23) gave back 1–2bp to 5.98%. Then the day's real event: at 13:30 the US reported a loss of 23,000 jobs against an expected 80,000 gain, with June revised down to +20,000 and wage growth slowing. Market rates fell promptly — gilt yields down as much as 4.4bp and the 1-year SONIA swap (the market's live gauge of where Bank Rate is heading) down 4.6bp at the low — before roughly two-thirds of the move faded by the close. Gilts finish the day down 0.9–1.9bp; the 1-year SONIA swap ends at 4.077%, −1.9bp. Two corrections were published today and stand noted: the gilt table now shows live intraday levels (fixed 14:05), and afternoon US releases shape Monday's fixing, not same-day rounds (corrected 13:46).
What it means for Monday
Our estimate of Monday morning's fixing ends the week at 5-year 5.496% (−0.4bp vs Friday's lunchtime fix), 10-year 5.974% (−0.6bp), 20-year 6.519% (−1.1bp). Treasurer's read: at lunchtime the case for waiting looked worth 3–4bp; by the close it has thinned to roughly a basis point — essentially level. A borrower with discretion loses little either way now; weekend headlines (Iran talks reportedly near a Hormuz deal, escalation in Ukraine) are the wildcard that could reset Monday's open in either direction. Labelled judgement, not a promise.
The week, and the week ahead
The week's shape: Thursday's sharp rise in borrowing costs (gilt yields up 4–6bp, PWLB rates following at Friday's AM fixing) and Friday's round trip on the US jobs shock. Net on the week, PWLB 10-year standard ends at 5.98% fixed, about 4bp above last Thursday's morning round. What markets expect from the Bank of England finishes the week: September on hold at 3.75%, the first rise still expected in November (to 4.00%), and the second around the turn of Q1 2027 — its exact timing flickered between March and April through Friday afternoon, a sign of how finely balanced that pricing is. Ahead: Monday's ~09:15 fixing is the next hard number; Thursday 07:00 UK brings preliminary Q2 GDP (quarterly growth forecast 0.2%, annual 1.6%); and US inflation data mid-week is the global event most likely to move UK rates.

An hour and a half after the weak US jobs report, rates are settling lower on the day: gilt yields down 1.8–3.8bp, and our estimate of Monday morning's PWLB rate sits 1.1–2.5bp below Friday's lunchtime fixing. Markets have also gently pushed back when they expect the Bank of England's second rate rise — April rather than March 2027.

Where rates stand this afternoon
Friday's arc so far: the morning fixing rose 4–6bp (10-year standard to 6.00%), the lunchtime round gave back 1–2bp (10-year 5.98%), and the weak US jobs report an hour later has pulled market rates below both. Gilt yields are down 1.8–3.8bp on the day, led by shorter maturities (2-year benchmark 4.249%, −3.8bp), and the one-year SONIA swap — a gauge of what markets expect the Bank of England to do — sits at 4.061%, −3.5bp. Our estimate of the next PWLB fixing (Monday ~09:15, today's rounds being done) is below Friday's lunchtime levels on every maturity: 5-year 5.475% vs 5.50% fixed, 10-year 5.960% vs 5.98%, 20-year 6.514% vs 6.53%. In plain terms: a borrower who did not lock at lunchtime has, so far, seen Monday's likely cost tick lower.
The world since lunch
Reuters confirms the shape of the US surprise — payrolls unexpectedly declining in July with unemployment easing to 4.1% — and separately reports the Japanese yen surging after the data, with traders wary of official intervention: a sign of how far the dollar move ran. MarketWatch is running live coverage of the jobs fallout. On the UK read-through, the Guardian's live blog reports that the odds of a September rate rise are falling — matching what the swap market shows: no move priced for September's meeting, the first rise still expected in November, and the second rise now expected in April 2027, a meeting later than this morning. Elsewhere, Russia has dropped a record number of glide bombs on Ukraine as casualties mount — grim, escalation-adjacent, and worth watching, though with limited direct gilt impact so far. Treasurer's read: the day's data pushed the whole expected rate path gently lower and later — supportive for borrowing costs at the margin, but one soft US print is not a trend.
Into the weekend
Nothing remains on today's UK calendar. The end-of-day summary lands ~17:30 UK; the next hard number for borrowers is Monday's ~09:15 fixing; and the week ahead is quiet until Thursday's preliminary Q2 GDP (07:00 UK, 13 August). Treasurer's read: if this afternoon's levels hold, Monday morning should price a few basis points below Friday — borrowers with timing discretion lose little by waiting, with the usual caveat that weekend news (Iran talks, Ukraine escalation) can reset the picture by Monday's open. Labelled judgement, not a promise.
